prompt.context: Our client is a for-profit, specialty college named Chic Cosmetology University (CCU). Founded in 2005, CCU is a program for high school graduates seeking their professional cosmetology license. CCU is currently the market leader for cosmetology education with campuses in ten major metropolitan areas in the US. CCU has capital to invest in a new campus and is considering Chicagoland as a location.
prompt.question: Should CCU open a new campus in Chicagoland?

clarifying_info.q: What does success look like for a new campus?
clarifying_info.a: The client considers a successful launch as achieving positive operating profit for the new campus two years after opening.

clarifying_info.q: How long do students take classes and when does the school year begin?
clarifying_info.a: Enrolled students take classes at a physical campus for one school year to earn their degree. The fiscal year begins on September 1.
CCU boasts the best campuses in the industry with state-of-the-art equipment and strong job placement due to relationships with top salons in local areas.

clarifying_info.q: Are CCU and industry enrollments growing?
clarifying_info.a: CCU and industry enrollments are growing at 5% per year.
There are 2-3 other large specialty colleges, some of which are in the same geographies as CCU. Community colleges are also beginning to offer cosmetology degrees at lower prices.

clarifying_info.q: How established are existing CCU campuses?
clarifying_info.a: All ten CCU campuses have been present for at least three full school years. All competitor campuses have also been present for similar lengths of time.

clarifying_info.q: What are the industry requirements to enter the field?
clarifying_info.a: A high school diploma and a cosmetology degree are required to enter the field. 98% of cosmetologists are women.

clarifying_info.q: What is the investment cost to build a new campus in Chicagoland?
clarifying_info.a: The total cost is $4.5M in initial building costs to renovate the chosen site. These costs can be amortized evenly over a three-year period. Fixed costs remain flat per year.

exhibits.title: 2010 CCU Financials
exhibits.shows: Income statement for all CCU campuses as of 8/31/2010, with student enrollments, revenue, fixed costs (buildings/equipment and recruiting/G&A), variable costs (instructors and student supplies), and operating profit, all in thousands of dollars.

exhibits.title: CCU and major competitor locations
exhibits.shows: A table showing CCU's 2010 market share (as a share of total potential students) at each of its ten campuses, alongside a map indicating the location of CCU campuses and major competitor campuses across the US.

data.note: Share measured as share of total potential students as defined by CCU; as of 8/31/2010

framework: Evaluate CCU's revenue and cost structure (revenue per student, fixed costs per campus, variable costs per student, gross profit per student)
Calculate break-even enrollment for the new Chicago campus, accounting for the initial investment amortization
Project the total addressable market of potential students in Chicagoland (HS-track and adult track)
Estimate CCU Chicago's realistic market share based on competitive dynamics from existing campuses
Determine projected Year 1 and Year 2 enrollments and compare to break-even
Identify qualitative factors and strategic alternatives

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 1, what is the average revenue per enrollment, total annual fixed cost per campus, total variable cost per student, and gross profit per student?
questions.guidance: Candidate should divide all-campus figures by 10 campuses or 10,000 students (note: enrollment figure of 10 in the exhibit is in thousands). Revenue per enrollment = $150M / 10K = $15K. Fixed cost per campus = $48M / 10 = $4.8M. Variable cost per student = $80M / 10K = $8K. Gross profit per student = $15K - $8K = $7K.

math.setup: All figures from Exhibit 1 are in $000s. Total campuses = 10. Total enrollments = 10 (000s) = 10,000 students.
steps: Total annual fixed cost per campus = $48,000K / 10 campuses = $4,800K = $4.8M
Total variable cost per student = $80,000K / 10,000 students = $8K
math.answer: Revenue per student = $15K; Fixed cost per campus = $4.8M; Variable cost per student = $8K; Gross profit per student = $7K

questions.prompt: What is the break-even number of students required for CCU Chicago in year 1?
questions.guidance: Candidate must add the amortized investment cost ($4.5M / 3 years = $1.5M per year) to the base fixed cost ($4.8M) to get total annual fixed costs of $6.3M, then divide by gross profit per student ($7K). Break-even = 900 students. Candidate should proactively ask about the investment cost before being told.

math.setup: Initial building cost = $4.5M, amortized evenly over 3 years = $1.5M per year. Annual fixed costs = base $4.8M + $1.5M amortization = $6.3M. Gross profit per student = $7K.

questions.prompt: What types of high schools and students do you think CCU targets?
questions.guidance: Strong candidates identify: public high schools (private HS grads more likely to attend 4-year university); high schools in middle-class cities (affordability concern for low-income); high schools geographically close to the campus; female high school graduates not attending a 4-year college who are interested in cosmetology. After a few criteria are noted, share that CCU has identified 1,000 targeted high schools in Chicagoland, and that within these HS, CCU's market research estimates on average 6 students per HS have potential for CCU enrollment.

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 2, what is the highest market share CCU Chicago could reasonably expect to capture in Year 1?
questions.guidance: Candidate should observe that campuses with competitors present tend to have lower share (~10%) than those without (~15%). Boston has 8% share with only one competitor, but that may be an outlier. The presence of more than one competitor does not have an incremental negative impact. Chicago has one competitor, so a 10% projected market share is appropriate. Excellent candidates note that all existing campuses have been in place for at least 3 years, so the 10% figure reflects a mature campus — a new campus in Year 1 is unlikely to achieve this immediately, making the case even harder. Also share: 80% of enrolled students come directly from high school, the other 20% come from the adult market.

questions.prompt: How many students should CCU Chicago expect to enroll in Year 1 at most?
questions.guidance: Candidate should calculate HS potential (6 students x 1,000 HS = 6,000), then adult potential (6,000 x 25% = 1,500 — note: adult market is 20% of total enrolled, meaning HS = 80%, so adult = 6,000 / 0.80 x 0.20 = 1,500, or equivalently 6,000 x 25%), giving total potential of 7,500. Apply 10% market share to get 750 students. Year 2 projection = 750 x 1.05 = 788 students. Both years fall below the 900 break-even threshold.

math.setup: Potential HS students = 6 per HS x 1,000 targeted HS = 6,000. Adult market = 20% of total enrolled (HS = 80%), so Adult potential = 6,000 / 80% x 20% = 1,500. Total potential = 7,500. Market share assumption = 10%.
steps: Potential (Adult) = 6,000 x 25% = 1,500 students (since adult = 20% and HS = 80% of total, adult = HS x 20/80)
math.answer: Year 1 = 750 students; Year 2 = 788 students — both below the 900 break-even

questions.prompt: (Bonus, if time permits) Suppose CCU finds a lot with a one-time construction cost of $300K with the same amortization schedule. Should they enter Chicago now?
questions.guidance: New amortization = $300K / 3 = $100K per year. Total fixed costs = $4.8M + $0.1M = $4.9M. New break-even = $4.9M / $7K = 700 students. At 750 projected enrollments, CCU would exceed break-even. However, an excellent candidate will note that the 10% market share used is based on mature campuses (3+ years established), so Year 1 is unlikely to reach 750 students, making even this scenario questionable.

math.setup: New one-time construction cost = $300K. Amortized over 3 years = $100K per year.
steps: Year 1 projected enrollment (700) vs break-even (700): marginally achievable on paper, but market share of 10% is for mature campuses and unlikely in Year 1
math.answer: New break-even = 700 students. Projected enrollment of 750 nominally exceeds this, but the 10% market share assumption is for established campuses; Year 1 share will likely be lower, so entry remains risky.

brainstorming.prompt: What qualitative issues should CCU consider?

categories.name: Demand-side strategies
ideas: Offer scholarships to increase the number of potential students and/or conversion rate of potential students
Target additional adult market segments beyond recent high school graduates
Partner with local salons for job placement to boost conversion rates

categories.name: Alternative market entry options
ideas: Consider other cities beyond Chicagoland that currently do not have a CCU presence
Add a second campus to a city such as NYC that has high market share and potentially low capacity
Perform market research in other cities to understand if potential per target high school is greater

categories.name: Cost reduction
ideas: Reduce fixed costs by transporting equipment and materials from campuses that are not at full capacity
Negotiate a lower-cost facility lease or renovation site
Share administrative resources across nearby campuses

categories.name: Competitive risk
ideas: Community colleges are beginning to offer cosmetology degrees at lower prices — risk of price-based competition
Existing competitor in Chicago may respond aggressively to CCU entry
New campus brand recognition will be low in Year 1 relative to established competitors

recommendation: CCU should NOT open the Chicago campus under the current cost structure. Even with an optimistic 10% market share, the campus would enroll only 750 students in Year 1 — 150 short of the 900 needed to break even. Year 2 (788 students) also falls below break-even.
Furthermore, the 10% market share benchmark is based on mature campuses with 3+ years of operation, so Year 1 share is likely to be even lower, making the shortfall worse than the base case suggests.
risks: Market share in Year 1 and Year 2 will likely be below 10% since benchmarks reflect mature (3+ year) campuses
One existing competitor in Chicago could intensify upon CCU entry
Community college competition on price could suppress enrollment
$4.5M initial investment is at risk if break-even is not achieved within two years
next_steps: Explore alternative locations with no existing competitor presence where CCU could capture 15%+ market share
Investigate whether a lower-cost facility (e.g., $300K construction) could bring break-even down to 700 students, but validate whether Year 1 market share can realistically reach 10%
Model a phased ramp-up scenario with realistic Year 1/Year 2 market share trajectories
Consider offering scholarships or partnerships to increase conversion of targeted students
Evaluate adding a second campus in a high-share, high-capacity city such as NYC instead
